title: Of giving the lie
paragraphs: But, someone will say to me, this project of making oneself the subject of one's own writing would be excusable in rare, famous men, who by their reputation had given others the curiosity to be fully informed about them. Quite true, I admit, and know very well, that a craftsman will scarcely lift his eyes from his work to look at an ordinary man, whereas he will leave his business and his shop to gawp at an eminent person when he comes into town. It ill suits anyone to give his own portrait but one who has qualities worthy of imitation, whose life and opinions can serve as an example: Caesar and Xenophon had a sound, solid foundation on which to base their narrations, in the greatness of their own deeds. And it is to be wished we had the journals of Alexander the Great, the commentaries that Augustus, Cato, Sulla, Brutus, and others left of their actions; men whose very statues, even in copper and marble, people love and contemplate. This objection is very true; but it concerns me very little:
"Non recito cuiquam, nisi amicis, idque coactus; Non ubivis, coramve quibuslibet, in medio qui Scripta foro recitant, sunt multi, quique lavantes."

["I recite my poems only to my friends, and only when forced to; not anywhere, before anyone — there are plenty who recite their writings in the middle of the marketplace and at the baths." — Horace, Sat., i. 4, 73.]
I am not setting up a statue here to be erected in a city's great square, in a church, or any public place:
"Non equidem hoc studeo, bullatis ut mihi nugis, Pagina turgescat...... Secreti loquimur:"
["I do not aim to swell my pages with empty trifles; you and I are talking in private." — Persius, Sat., v. 19.]

It is for some corner of a library, or to entertain a neighbour, a relative, a friend who has a mind to renew his acquaintance and intimacy with me in this image of myself. Others have been encouraged to speak of themselves because they found the subject worthy and rich; I, on the contrary, am the bolder because the subject is so poor and barren that I cannot be suspected of ostentation. I judge freely of others' actions; I give little of my own to be judged, because they are nothing. I do not find so much good in myself that I cannot tell it without blushing.

What contentment it would be to me if someone could tell me about the manners, faces, expressions, ordinary words, and fortunes of my ancestors! How attentively I should listen! In earnest, it would be ill-natured to despise so much as the pictures of our friends and predecessors, the fashion of their clothes and arms. I preserve their writing, seal, and a particular sword they wore, and have not thrown out of my study the long staves my father used to carry in his hand.
"Paterna vestis, et annulus, tanto charior est posteris, quanto erga parentes major affectus."
["A father's garment and ring is so much the dearer to his descendants as their affection towards their parents is the greater." — St Augustine, De Civitate Dei, i. 13.]

If my posterity is nevertheless of another mind, I shall be avenged: they cannot care less for me than I shall then care for them. All the dealings I have with the public in this matter is that I borrow their tools of writing, which are easier and most at hand; and in return I shall perhaps keep a pound of butter from melting in the sun in the market:
"Ne toga cordyllis, ne penula desit olivis; Et laxas scombris saepe dabo tunicas;"
["Lest wrappers be wanting for tunny-fish, or coverings for olives; and I shall often supply loose tunics for mackerel." — Martial, xiii. 1, 1.]

And even if nobody were to read me — have I wasted my time by entertaining myself for so many idle hours in such pleasant and useful thoughts? In moulding this figure upon myself, I have so often been forced to compose myself in proper posture that the copy has been truly drawn, and has in some sort formed itself. Painting myself for others, I have represented myself in better colouring than my own natural complexion. I have no more made my book than my book has made me — it is a book consubstantial with its author, of a peculiar design, a part of my life, whose business is not designed for others, as is the business of all other books. In giving myself such a continual and exact account of myself, have I lost my time? For those who only sometimes survey themselves cursorily do not examine themselves so strictly, nor penetrate so deep, as the man who makes it his business, his study, and his employment — who intends a lasting record, with all his fidelity and all his force. The most delicious pleasures, digested within, leave no trace of themselves and avoid the sight not only of the people, but of any other person. How often this work has diverted me from troublesome thoughts! And all that are frivolous should be reckoned troublesome. Nature has given us a large faculty for entertaining ourselves alone, and often calls us to it, to teach us that we owe ourselves in part to society, but chiefly and mostly to ourselves. To accustom my imagination even to meditate in some method and to some end, and to keep it from losing itself and roving at random, it is enough to give body to and record all the little thoughts that present themselves to it. I lend an ear to my whims because I am to record them. It often happens that, being displeased at some action that civility and reason will not let me openly reprove, I disgorge myself here — not without an eye to public instruction. And these poetical lashes,
"Zon zur l'oeil, ion sur le groin, Zon zur le dos du Sagoin,"
["A slap on his eye, a slap on his snout, a slap on Sagoin's back." — Marot, Fripelippes, Valet de Marot à Sagoin.]

imprint themselves better on paper than on flesh. What if I listen a little more attentively than usual to books, watching whether I can pilfer anything that might adorn or support my own? I have not in the least studied to make a book; but I have in some way studied because I had made it — if it is studying to scratch and pinch now one author and then another, either by the head or by the foot, not with any intention of forming opinions from them, but to assist, support, and fortify those I have already embraced. But whom shall we believe in the report he makes of himself, in so corrupt an age — considering that there are so few, if any, whom we can believe when speaking of others, where there is less interest in lying? The first thing done in the corruption of manners is the banishing of truth; for, as Pindar says, to be true is the beginning of a great virtue, and the first article that Plato requires in the governor of his Republic. The truth of these days is not what really is, but what every man persuades another man to believe; just as we give the name of money not only to genuine coin, but to false coin too, if it will pass. Our nation has long been reproached with this vice; for Salvianus of Marseilles, who lived in the time of the Emperor Valentinian, says that lying and perjury are with the French not a vice but a way of speaking. Anyone wishing to push this testimony further might say that today it is a virtue with them; men form and fashion themselves to it as to an exercise of honour, for dissimulation is one of the most notable qualities of this age.

I have often wondered where this custom we so religiously observe sprang from — of being more highly offended by the reproach of a vice so familiar to us than by any other, and of holding it the greatest insult that words can do us to be called a liar. Looking into it, I find it natural to defend most strongly those defects with which we are most tainted. It seems as if by resenting and being moved at the accusation, we somehow acquit ourselves of the fault; though we have it in effect, we condemn it in outward appearance. May it not also be that this reproach seems to imply cowardice and feebleness of heart? Of which can there be a more manifest sign than to eat one's own words — nay, to lie against one's own knowledge? Lying is a base vice; a vice that one of the ancients portrays in the most odious colours when he says that "to lie is to manifest a contempt of God, and at the same time a fear of men." It is not possible to represent more fully the horror, baseness, and irregularity of it; for what can a man imagine more hateful and contemptible than to be a coward toward men and brave against his Maker? Our intelligence being communicable from one to another only through the particular instrument of words, he who falsifies that betrays public society. It is the only way by which we communicate our thoughts and our wills; it is the interpreter of the soul; if it deceives us, we no longer know nor have any further hold on one another; if it deceives us, it breaks all our correspondence and dissolves all the ties of government. Certain peoples of the newly discovered Indies (I need not name them, since they are no more; for, by extraordinary and unheard-of example, the desolation of that conquest extended to the utter abolition of names and the ancient knowledge of places) offered to their gods human blood, but only such as was drawn from the tongue and the ears, to expiate the sin of lying, as well heard as spoken. That good fellow of Greece said that children are amused with toys, and men with words.

As to our various practices of giving the lie, and the laws of honour in such cases, and the changes they have undergone, I postpone to another time what I have to say about them; and shall learn, if I can, in the meantime, when the custom began of so exactly weighing and measuring words, and of making our honour invested in them. For it is easy to judge that it was not anciently so among the Romans and Greeks. And it has often seemed strange to me to see them rail at each other and give one another the lie without any quarrel. Their laws of duty steered a different course from ours. Caesar is sometimes called thief, sometimes drunkard, to his face. We see the freedom of invective they practised on one another — I mean the greatest war-chiefs of both nations — where words were revenged only with words and went no further.
